title: Nonreversible Gauge Fields in Fokker--Planck Dynamics: Supersymmetric Hamiltonians and Learned Finite Forces
summary: We formulate stationary-density-preserving nonreversible perturbations of Fokker--Planck dynamics as gauge fields that deform relaxation spectra while leaving the invariant state fixed. When detailed balance holds, a similarity transformation maps the reversible Fokker--Planck operator to a Witten-Laplacian-type supersymmetric Hamiltonian; nonreversible gauges then appear as non-Hermitian perturbations that preserve the zero mode but modify the excited spectrum. This operator viewpoint gives a common language for relaxation gaps, circulating probability currents, hypocoercive acceleration, and finite control costs. We represent admissible gauge currents by antisymmetric tensor fields and identify the detailed-balance-violating Ohzeki--Ichiki force as a constant symplectic example whose infinite-strength limit is Hamiltonian dynamics. The continuous-time spectral gap alone does not select a finite gauge strength, so we introduce a finite-time regularized objective and an actor--critic procedure for learning the gauge. An exactly solvable anisotropic Gaussian Ornstein--Uhlenbeck benchmark separates the spectral transition from the finite-time optimum and shows that the learned gauge recovers the Lyapunov-equation optimum. A double-well benchmark then illustrates the same constrained selection in a nonconvex metastable landscape. Stochastic gradient methods enter this framework as physically relevant Fokker--Planck systems: mini-batch noise acts as an effective diffusion tensor, and adaptive methods such as Adam correspond to metric choices with possible nonequilibrium currents.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates nonreversible perturbations of Fokker-Planck dynamics as gauge fields that preserve the stationary state but modify relaxation spectra. It connects this to supersymmetric Hamiltonians, hypocoercive acceleration, and optimal control, then proposes a regularized objective and actor-critic method for learning the gauge, demonstrated on Gaussian and double-well benchmarks, with connections to stochastic gradient methods like Adam.
AI.motivation: To provide a unified operator-theoretic framework for understanding and learning nonreversible, stationary-density-preserving perturbations of Fokker-Planck dynamics, bridging concepts from relaxation spectra, probability currents, hypocoercive acceleration, and control costs.
AI.method: The paper uses similarity transformations to map reversible Fokker-Planck operators to Witten-Laplacian-type supersymmetric Hamiltonians, introduces antisymmetric tensor fields to represent admissible gauge currents, and proposes a finite-time regularized objective with an actor-critic algorithm for learning the optimal gauge. Benchmarks include anisotropic Gaussian Ornstein-Uhlenbeck and double-well systems.
AI.result: The continuous-time spectral gap does not uniquely determine the optimal gauge strength; finite-time regularization resolves this. The learned gauge recovers the Lyapunov-equation optimum in the Gaussian case. The framework connects to stochastic gradient methods: mini-batch noise acts as effective diffusion, and Adam corresponds to metric choices with nonequilibrium currents.
AI.conclusion: Nonreversible gauge perturbations offer a principled and learnable approach to accelerate convergence in Fokker-Planck systems while preserving the stationary distribution, with natural links to optimization algorithms.

title: Reply to "Interpreting Bohm quantum potentials in `Computing quantum waves exactly from classical action'"
comment: Comment on arXiv:2605.20443, 3 pages, no figures
summary: The recent arXiv posting arXiv:2605.20443 by Lohmiller and Slotine attempts to address the omission of the Bohm quantum potential in their proposed exact equivalence between classical action and the Schrödinger equation. They introduce a position-dependent time transformation to argue that the spatial derivatives of the probability density amplitude vanish for the Feynman kernel. A rigorous mathematical examination of this transformation reveals a violation of the multivariable chain rule. The spatial derivatives do not vanish in the physical reference frame. The mathematical framework presented by the authors remains identical to the well-established semiclassical Van Vleck propagator, which is exact exclusively for quadratic potentials.

AI.tldr: This paper refutes a recent arXiv claim (2605.20443) that a position-dependent time transformation eliminates the Bohm quantum potential from the Feynman kernel, showing it violates the multivariable chain rule and reduces to the standard semiclassical Van Vleck propagator valid only for quadratic potentials.
AI.motivation: To critically examine and refute the claim by Lohmiller and Slotine (arXiv:2605.20443) that a position-dependent time transformation can eliminate the Bohm quantum potential from the Feynman kernel, thereby establishing an exact equivalence between classical action and the Schrödinger equation.
AI.method: A rigorous mathematical examination of the position-dependent time transformation proposed in arXiv:2605.20443, focusing on the application of the multivariable chain rule to the spatial derivatives of the probability density amplitude in the Feynman kernel.
AI.result: The proposed transformation violates the multivariable chain rule; spatial derivatives do not vanish in the physical reference frame. The mathematical framework is identical to the semiclassical Van Vleck propagator, which is exact only for quadratic potentials.
AI.conclusion: The claim of an exact equivalence between classical action and the Schrödinger equation via the proposed transformation is mathematically unsound, as the Bohm quantum potential remains non-vanishing for non-quadratic potentials.

title: Programmable spectral symmetries in an anisotropic quantum Rabi simulator
summary: The quantum Rabi model captures fundamental aspects of light--matter interaction, where symmetry dictates both spectra and dynamics. Over the past years, experiments have explored many of its nonperturbative properties, but have mostly focused on the isotropic limit, where rotating and counterrotating processes are locked together, leaving the broader symmetry landscape largely unexplored. Here we realize a programmable anisotropic quantum Rabi model in a superconducting processor, with independent control of the rotating and counterrotating couplings $(g_1,g_2)$ and of a transverse bias $\varepsilon$. Continuous anisotropy tuning, combined with a duality mapping, gives access to the full parameter space from the Jaynes-Cummings to the anti-Jaynes-Cummings limits. In the deep-strong-coupling regime, we show that anisotropy reconstructs the spectrum and turns complete collapse-revival dynamics into incomplete revivals even near degeneracy. With adiabatic state preparation and joint tomography, we resolve an anisotropy-induced ground-state parity switch, a crossing that has no analogue in the isotropic model. We further observe selective tunnelling associated with hidden symmetry in biased Rabi models and track its anisotropic displacement within the same device. These results establish a controllable route to engineering nonperturbative light--matter Hamiltonians, where symmetry, spectrum, and dynamics can be programmed independently.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the experimental realization of a programmable anisotropic quantum Rabi model in a superconducting processor, enabling independent control of rotating and counterrotating couplings. The authors demonstrate continuous anisotropy tuning, observe anisotropy-induced ground-state parity switching, selective tunnelling from hidden symmetry, and modified collapse-revival dynamics in the deep-strong-coupling regime.
AI.motivation: Previous experiments on the quantum Rabi model have mostly focused on the isotropic limit where rotating and counterrotating couplings are locked together, leaving the broader symmetry landscape unexplored. The authors aim to realize a fully programmable anisotropic quantum Rabi model to access the complete parameter space and explore symmetry-controlled phenomena.
AI.method: The authors implement the anisotropic quantum Rabi model in a superconducting processor with independent control of rotating coupling $g_1$, counterrotating coupling $g_2$, and transverse bias $\varepsilon$. They use continuous anisotropy tuning combined with a duality mapping to access the full parameter space, and employ adiabatic state preparation and joint tomography for characterization.
AI.result: They observe: (1) anisotropic reconstruction of the spectrum in the deep-strong-coupling regime, turning complete collapse-revival dynamics into incomplete revivals; (2) an anisotropy-induced ground-state parity switch with no analogue in the isotropic model; (3) selective tunnelling associated with hidden symmetry in biased Rabi models and its anisotropic displacement.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a controllable route to engineering nonperturbative light-matter Hamiltonians where symmetry, spectrum, and dynamics can be programmed independently, opening access to previously unexplored symmetry landscapes in quantum optics and simulation.

title: Frustrated superradiant phases in one- and two-dimensional lattices
summary: Understanding how frustration and symmetry breaking shape collective behavior is a central problem in quantum many-body systems. In this work, we investigate this problem in large one- and two-dimensional arrays of coupled Dicke models on a periodic lattice, where strong light-matter coupling gives rise to a superradiant phase and competition between neighboring order parameters induces spontaneous translational symmetry breaking. Such Dicke lattice models constitute a fundamentally new class of quantum many-body systems, as they simultaneously realize the thermodynamic limit associated with the lattice size and an intrinsic thermodynamic limit arising from collective on-site interactions with quantum emitters. We show that frustration drives photonic density-wave ordering, and that the resulting broken periodicity can be predicted from the excitation spectrum of the symmetric phase, without requiring computationally prohibitive thermodynamic energy minimization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an emergent Nambu-Goldstone mode arises near the critical point in a one-dimensional chain despite the presence of only discrete symmetry, and uncover the mechanism that enables this otherwise forbidden gapless excitation. We also find quasi-periodic ordering in the superradiant phase, reminiscent of quasicrystals, and demonstrate that synthetic magnetic flux provides a powerful knob to control the nature of translational symmetry breaking. Our results establish a new direction in quantum many-body physics where the coexistence of local and global thermodynamic limits gives rise to unconventional symmetry breaking and emergent collective behavior.

AI.tldr: This work investigates frustration and symmetry breaking in large 1D and 2D arrays of coupled Dicke models, showing that frustration drives photonic density-wave ordering, an emergent Nambu-Goldstone mode arises near criticality in 1D despite only discrete symmetry, and synthetic magnetic flux can control translational symmetry breaking.
AI.motivation: To understand how frustration and symmetry breaking shape collective behavior in quantum many-body systems, specifically in coupled Dicke lattice models that simultaneously realize two thermodynamic limits (lattice size and on-site collective interactions).
AI.method: The authors analyze large one- and two-dimensional arrays of coupled Dicke models on a periodic lattice, studying the excitation spectrum of the symmetric phase to predict broken periodicity without thermodynamic energy minimization.
AI.result: (1) Frustration drives photonic density-wave ordering. (2) Broken periodicity can be predicted from the excitation spectrum of the symmetric phase. (3) An emergent Nambu-Goldstone mode arises near the critical point in 1D despite only discrete symmetry. (4) Quasi-periodic ordering (reminiscent of quasicrystals) appears in the superradiant phase. (5) Synthetic magnetic flux controls translational symmetry breaking.
AI.conclusion: The coexistence of local and global thermodynamic limits in Dicke lattice models enables unconventional symmetry breaking and emergent collective behavior, establishing a new direction in quantum many-body physics.

title: Emergent Self-Similar Quantum Revivals in Spiral Drives
summary: We uncover a distinct form of nonequilibrium temporal order: self-similar quantum revivals in a many-body system driven by quasiperiodic spiral kicks, where the system recurrently returns close to its initial state at a hierarchically nested sequence of times. We demonstrate that both the fidelity and entanglement entropy exhibit this self-similar temporal structure. It originates from an emergent dynamical attractor, which we identify, such that all momentum modes eventually fall into the same closed orbits at self-similar times. We analytically justify this behavior and show that, for special momentum modes, this attractor arises as a consequence of a generalized spin echo process, and more generally we prove its existence using quasiperiodic SU(2) cocycles. Interestingly, the dynamics between consecutive revivals supports either volume- or area-law entanglement scaling, tunable via the driving parameters. In the presence of integrability-breaking perturbations, the system eventually heats up, but a long-lived prethermal regime with algebraically tunable lifetime occurs before heating sets in. Our results establish self-similar quantum revivals as a new paradigm for nonequilibrium quantum matter and provide a realistic route for its observation in current quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: This paper discovers self-similar quantum revivals in a many-body system driven by quasiperiodic spiral kicks, where the system returns close to its initial state at hierarchically nested times, with fidelity and entanglement entropy both exhibiting this self-similar structure. The behavior originates from an emergent dynamical attractor, analytically justified via generalized spin echo and quasiperiodic SU(2) cocycles, and shows tunable entanglement scaling (volume- or area-law) and a long-lived prethermal regime under integrability-breaking perturbations.
AI.motivation: To uncover and characterize a distinct form of nonequilibrium temporal order—self-similar quantum revivals—in driven many-body systems, and to establish it as a new paradigm for nonequilibrium quantum matter with realistic prospects for experimental observation.
AI.method: Analytical derivation using generalized spin echo processes and quasiperiodic SU(2) cocycles; numerical demonstration of fidelity and entanglement entropy revivals; identification of an emergent dynamical attractor where all momentum modes fall into closed orbits at self-similar times.
AI.result: Self-similar quantum revivals are shown to occur, with both fidelity and entanglement entropy displaying hierarchical temporal structure. The intervening dynamics supports tunable entanglement scaling (volume-law or area-law). Under integrability-breaking perturbations, a prethermal regime with algebraically tunable lifetime is observed before eventual heating.
AI.conclusion: Self-similar quantum revivals represent a new paradigm for nonequilibrium quantum matter, with a realistic route for observation in current quantum simulators.

title: Isospectrality and Operator Complexity
summary: We study a pair of exactly solvable, isospectral fermion chains, one strongly interacting and one quadratic, that nevertheless display remarkably different phase structures and operator dynamics. A nonlocal nonlinear unitary transformation maps one onto the other while preserving the entire many-body spectrum and converting local fermion operators into extended many-body strings. Thus, operators that evolve within a closed linear subspace in the quadratic model become interacting operators that generate increasingly higher-body terms and exhibit asymptotic Lanczos growth $b_n\propto\sqrt n$. Despite their identical spectra, the two models realize distinct phases and sharply different notions of operator complexity. Our results demonstrate that free many-body spectra and interacting operator dynamics are fundamentally compatible.

AI.tldr: Two isospectral fermion chains (one strongly interacting, one quadratic) connected by a nonlocal unitary transformation exhibit identical spectra but vastly different phase structures and operator dynamics, with the interacting model showing asymptotic Lanczos growth b_n ∝ √n and increasingly higher-body terms.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that free many-body spectra and interacting operator dynamics are fundamentally compatible, challenging conventional assumptions about the relationship between spectral properties and operator complexity.
AI.method: Study a pair of exactly solvable, isospectral fermion chains connected by a nonlocal nonlinear unitary transformation that preserves the many-body spectrum while converting local fermion operators into extended many-body strings.
AI.result: Operators in the quadratic model evolve within a closed linear subspace, while in the interacting model they generate increasingly higher-body terms with asymptotic Lanczos growth b_n ∝ √n. Despite identical spectra, the two models realize distinct phases and sharply different operator complexity.
AI.conclusion: Free many-body spectra and interacting operator dynamics can coexist; spectral equivalence does not imply equivalent operator growth or phase structure.

title: Continuous-variable ADAPT-VQE for bosonic lattice models
summary: We present a continuous-variable adaptive variational quantum eigensolver (CV-ADAPT-VQE). As concrete examples, we consider the ground-state preparation for (i) the Bose-Hubbard model and (ii) the bosonic Kitaev chain, including its extension with an on-site Kerr interaction. The former conserves the total boson number, while the latter conserves global parity. We construct symmetry-preserving operator pools tailored to each case and show, using GPU-based classical simulations, that CV-ADAPT-VQE results in significantly shallower circuits compared to Hamiltonian-based VQE approaches. Our results point toward direct applications in quantum simulations of condensed-matter systems, quantum chemistry, and high-energy physics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CV-ADAPT-VQE, a continuous-variable adaptive variational quantum eigensolver, and demonstrates its efficiency for ground-state preparation of the Bose-Hubbard model and the bosonic Kitaev chain, achieving shallower circuits than Hamiltonian-based VQE approaches via symmetry-preserving operator pools.
AI.motivation: To develop a more efficient variational quantum eigensolver for continuous-variable systems that generates shallower circuits compared to Hamiltonian-based approaches, enabling practical quantum simulations of bosonic systems.
AI.method: CV-ADAPT-VQE: an adaptive variational quantum eigensolver that constructs symmetry-preserving operator pools tailored to specific bosonic systems; demonstrated via GPU-based classical simulations on the Bose-Hubbard model (boson number conserving) and bosonic Kitaev chain (parity conserving).
AI.result: CV-ADAPT-VQE produces significantly shallower circuits compared to Hamiltonian-based VQE approaches for both the Bose-Hubbard model and the bosonic Kitaev chain (including with Kerr interaction).
AI.conclusion: The method has direct applications in quantum simulations of condensed-matter systems, quantum chemistry, and high-energy physics.

title: Setting angles in quantum approximate optimization at utility-scale
summary: The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is a powerful heuristic that seeks to solve combinatorial optimization problems using quantum hardware and classical optimization in tandem. Various methods exist to train the parameterized quantum circuits that serve as an ansatz in QAOA. However, which method works best to identify optimal angles for a given problem instance remains poorly understood, especially at utility-scale, i.e., $100$ qubits or more. In this work, we address this challenge through utility-scale benchmarks from which we distill operational guidance for QAOA practitioners. First, we investigate approximation techniques, such as matrix product states and Pauli propagation, to find optimal angles. Second, we train QAOA on small-scale representative problems and transfer the angles to larger ones. We then validate the results on quantum hardware for utility-scale problem instances that can be meaningfully executed. In this way, we identify insights for QAOA angle setting strategies that work best for problems at the utility scale, including as a function of resource cost for the search. Crucially, the operational implications we draw from our benchmarks will help quantum optimization practitioners execute QAOA end-to-end pipelines efficiently on current and future hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks strategies for training QAOA at utility scale (100+ qubits), finding that approximation techniques (matrix product states, Pauli propagation) and small-to-large angle transfer work best, providing operational guidance for practitioners on current and future quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: Despite QAOA's promise as a heuristic for combinatorial optimization, it is poorly understood which training methods identify optimal angles at utility scale (100+ qubits), motivating the need for systematic benchmarks and operational guidance.
AI.method: The authors benchmark QAOA angle-setting strategies using (1) approximation techniques like matrix product states and Pauli propagation for finding optimal angles, and (2) training on small-scale representative problems then transferring angles to larger instances. They validate results on quantum hardware for utility-scale problem instances.
AI.result: They identify which QAOA angle setting strategies work best at utility scale, including how performance depends on resource cost for the search, and provide actionable insights validated on real quantum hardware.
AI.conclusion: The operational implications from these benchmarks will help quantum optimization practitioners execute efficient end-to-end QAOA pipelines on current and future quantum hardware.

title: Feature Encoding in Quantum Machine Learning: A Survey and Practical Guidelines
comment: Article submitted to ACM Computer Surveys the 15-Apr-2026
summary: The encoding of classical data into quantum states constitutes the primary performance bottleneck in Quantum Machine Learning (qml) on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (nisq) devices. No existing framework jointly characterises resource cost, expressivity, and noise robustness, nor provides actionable selection guidelines for practitioners. This survey addresses that gap through a systematic review of 66 primary works (2017-2026) assembled via a PRISMA-adapted protocol across five academic databases. Four principal contributions are made. First, a three-axis cost-expressivity-robustness taxonomy classifies all major encoding families - basis, angle, dense-angle, amplitude, data re-uploading, and IQP - along independently measurable axes. Second, closed-form depth-fidelity bounds under nisq decoherence channels identify the critical gate-error rate p* ~ 10^-3 below which amplitude encoding is viable. Third, a unified treatment of Fourier expressivity, barren-plateau onset, and quantum kernel concentration as functions of the encoding circuit provides the first joint trainability analysis. Fourth, a five-regime decision framework maps (D, n, p, tau) - feature dimension, qubit budget, error rate, and task type - to a hardware-grounded encoding recommendation. The central finding is that for p >= 10^-3, shallow angle-based encodings consistently outperform amplitude encoding in practice, despite the latter's exponential qubit advantage.

AI.tldr: This survey systematically reviews 66 works (2017-2026) on quantum encoding for QML on NISQ devices, proposing a cost-expressivity-robustness taxonomy, closed-form fidelity bounds under decoherence, joint trainability analysis, and a five-regime decision framework mapping feature dimension, qubit budget, error rate, and task type to optimal encoding choices. The key finding: for gate-error rates p ≥ 10⁻³, shallow angle-based encodings outperform amplitude encoding despite the latter's exponential qubit advantage.
AI.motivation: Existing frameworks do not jointly characterize resource cost, expressivity, and noise robustness of quantum encodings, nor provide actionable selection guidelines for practitioners, creating a critical gap in QML on NISQ devices.
AI.method: PRISMA-adapted systematic review of 66 primary works across five academic databases; construction of a three-axis cost-expressivity-robustness taxonomy; derivation of closed-form depth-fidelity bounds under NISQ decoherence channels; unified analysis of Fourier expressivity, barren-plateau onset, and quantum kernel concentration; development of a five-regime decision framework mapping (D, n, p, τ) to encoding recommendations.
AI.result: Identified critical gate-error rate p* ~ 10⁻³ as the viability threshold for amplitude encoding; demonstrated that for p ≥ 10⁻³, shallow angle-based encodings consistently outperform amplitude encoding in practice; provided first joint trainability analysis linking Fourier expressivity, barren plateau, and kernel concentration to encoding circuit structure.
AI.conclusion: A five-regime decision framework provides hardware-grounded encoding recommendations based on feature dimension, qubit budget, error rate, and task type, offering practitioners a systematic approach to encoding selection in NISQ-era QML.

title: Multi-Qubit Dyadic Phase Fixing for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Compilation
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires translating application-level quantum circuits into the Clifford+$T$ gate set, where the $T$ gate is the dominant resource cost. Phase kickback is an ancilla-based technique that can dramatically reduce $T$-count for rotations with dyadic angles, but has previously been limited to highly structured circuit families. We present Dyadic Phase Fixing (DPF), a general multi-qubit synthesis tool that extends phase kickback to general quantum circuits. DPF uses numerical unitary synthesis to greedily extract dyadic angle rotations from any input circuit. Combined with a decision matrix to automatically size the final phase gradient register, our end-to-end workflow achieves up to 70% reduction in $T$-count compared to \texttt{gridsynth} and up to 60% compared to Repeat-Until-Success synthesis on a diverse set of benchmarks. We map these compiled circuits to a surface-code architecture to evaluate space-time volume, demonstrating up to a 60\% reduction in this metric as well. However, for some circuits and mapping strategies the two metrics diverge significantly, demonstrating that $T$-count alone is a useful but incomplete proxy for fault-tolerant program costs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Dyadic Phase Fixing (DPF), a general multi-qubit synthesis tool that extends phase kickback to arbitrary quantum circuits, achieving up to 70% T-count reduction over gridsynth and up to 60% reduction over Repeat-Until-Success synthesis, with corresponding space-time volume improvements of up to 60% on surface-code architectures.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires translating circuits into Clifford+T gates where T gates dominate resource cost; existing phase kickback techniques reduce T-count but are limited to highly structured circuit families.
AI.method: DPF uses numerical unitary synthesis to greedily extract dyadic angle rotations from any input circuit, combined with a decision matrix to automatically size the final phase gradient register.
AI.result: Up to 70% T-count reduction vs gridsynth, up to 60% vs Repeat-Until-Success synthesis, and up to 60% space-time volume reduction on surface-code architecture across diverse benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: DPF generalizes phase kickback to arbitrary circuits with significant resource reductions, though T-count and space-time volume can diverge for some circuits, indicating T-count alone is an incomplete proxy for fault-tolerant costs.

title: On the Cryptographic Structure Required for Verifying Qubits
summary:
Classically testing for the presence of anti-commuting operators on a quantum device is a critical tool underpinning recent progress in classical verification of quantum computation. While such tests can be based on cryptographic assumptions, known constructions rely on highly structured assumptions, e.g. trapdoor claw-free functions.
  In this work, we seek to explain this state of affairs by constructing strong cryptography from (certain forms of) classical tests of anti-commutation. In particular, we formulate the notion of a test of non-commutation (ToNC), an interactive protocol between a quantum prover and classical verifier in which the prover's final-round response is obtained by measuring one of two binary observables $P_0,P_1$ depending on the verifier's challenge bit $c$. We prove that, for a broad range of parameters, ToNC implies classical-communication key agreement (KA), and ToNC combined with one-way functions implies oblivious transfer (OT).
  Along the way, we develop tools for and provide the first known results on hardness amplification for post-quantum KA and OT, where communication is classical but adversaries may be quantum. In particular, we prove the following results of independent interest.
  - Post-quantum hard-core measure theorem: For any efficiently sampleable high-min-entropy distribution $D$ over pairs $(x,b)$ such that quantum circuits have advantage at most $δ$ in predicting $b$ from $x$, there exists a sub-distribution $M\preceq D$ of density $(1-δ)$ on which $b$ is nearly optimally quantum-hard to predict.
  - Post-quantum interactive XOR lemma: Given any classically-interactive protocol, if quantum adversaries have advantage at most $δ$ in guessing a private challenger bit $b$, then two sequential repetitions reduce the advantage for predicting the XOR of the challenger bits $b_1\oplus b_2$ to at most $δ^2+\rm{negl}(λ)$.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that classical tests of anti-commutation (ToNC) imply key agreement and, combined with one-way functions, oblivious transfer. It also develops hardness amplification tools for post-quantum cryptography: a hard-core measure theorem and an interactive XOR lemma for quantum adversaries.
AI.motivation: To explain why existing classical verification of quantum computation tests rely on highly structured cryptographic assumptions (e.g., trapdoor claw-free functions) by showing that such tests inherently imply strong cryptography (key agreement and oblivious transfer).
AI.method: Formalizes the notion of a Test of Non-Commutation (ToNC), an interactive protocol where a quantum prover measures one of two binary observables based on a verifier's challenge bit. Proves that ToNC implies classical-communication key agreement (KA), and ToNC + one-way functions implies oblivious transfer (OT). Develops two technical tools: a post-quantum hard-core measure theorem and a post-quantum interactive XOR lemma.
AI.result: ToNC (for a broad range of parameters) implies classical-communication key agreement. ToNC combined with one-way functions implies oblivious transfer. First known hardness amplification results for post-quantum KA and OT: the hard-core measure theorem extracts a sub-distribution where a bit is nearly optimally hard to predict, and the interactive XOR lemma shows XOR of two sequential repetitions reduces advantage from δ to δ² + negligible.
AI.conclusion: Classical tests of anti-commutation are inherently cryptographic: they imply key agreement and, with one-way functions, oblivious transfer. The new hardness amplification tools enable further reductions in post-quantum settings.

title: A Class of Multipartite Entangled States Based on State Transitions
summary: We introduce Transition states (T states), denoted by $\ket{T_k^n}$, as a class of multipartite entangled states characterized by a fixed number of state transitions between adjacent qubits. These states form equal-amplitude superpositions over all states with a specified transition count. Unlike Bell states based on two-qubit correlations, GHZ states characterized by global correlations among all qubits, and W and Dicke states based on fixed numbers of qubit excitations, T states are defined by transition counts along an ordered sequence of qubits. We prove that T states are unitarily equivalent to Dicke states through a chain of CX (controlled-X) operations, thereby establishing a direct correspondence between transition-based and excitation-based representations of multipartite entanglement.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Transition states (T states), a new class of multipartite entangled states defined by fixed transition counts between adjacent qubits. T states are shown to be unitarily equivalent to Dicke states via CX operations, bridging transition-based and excitation-based entanglement representations.
AI.motivation: To define a new class of multipartite entangled states (T states) based on transition counts between adjacent qubits, distinguishing them from existing entanglement classes (Bell, GHZ, W, Dicke) that rely on correlations or excitation counts.
AI.method: T states are constructed as equal-amplitude superpositions over all basis states with a specified number of qubit transitions. Unitary equivalence to Dicke states is proven using a chain of CX (controlled-X) operations.
AI.result: T states are unitarily equivalent to Dicke states via a chain of CX operations, establishing a formal correspondence between transition-based and excitation-based multipartite entanglement.
AI.conclusion: T states provide a novel transition-based perspective on multipartite entanglement, with direct structural links to the well-known Dicke states, offering an alternative framework for understanding entanglement in ordered qubit systems.

title: Quantum Radar Cross Section with two-photon entangled states
summary: We study two-photon entangled states for quantum radar cross section (QRCS), which is an extension of a single-photon QRCS formula. Since signal-idler entanglement does not provide any enhancement of the QRCS [Brandsema's PhD Thesis (2017)], we focus on signal-signal entanglement and derive the corresponding biphoton QRCS. We show that it can provide an enhancement over the single-photon QRCS and two-photon separable QRCS, where the performance is evaluated for various two-dimensional target geometries in monostatic/bistatic configurations. Furthermore, using the double-Gaussian approximation, we derive QRCS formula for biphoton states with arbitrary degree of entanglement and compute the resulting scattering patterns.

AI.tldr: This paper studies two-photon entangled states for quantum radar cross section (QRCS), focusing on signal-signal entanglement rather than signal-idler entanglement. The authors derive a biphoton QRCS formula that can provide enhancement over single-photon and two-photon separable QRCS, evaluating performance for various 2D target geometries in monostatic/bistatic configurations. Using double-Gaussian approximation, they derive QRCS for biphoton states with arbitrary entanglement degree.
AI.motivation: To extend single-photon QRCS to biphoton entangled states and investigate whether entanglement can provide enhancement in quantum radar cross section, specifically addressing the limitation that signal-idler entanglement does not yield QRCS improvement.
AI.method: Derivation of biphoton QRCS formula for signal-signal entangled states; evaluation for various two-dimensional target geometries in monostatic and bistatic configurations; use of double-Gaussian approximation to derive QRCS formula for biphoton states with arbitrary degree of entanglement.
AI.result: Signal-signal biphoton entanglement can provide enhancement over single-photon QRCS and two-photon separable QRCS.
AI.conclusion: Biphoton entangled states with signal-signal entanglement offer a viable pathway for improving quantum radar cross section performance beyond what is achievable with single-photon or separable two-photon states.

title: Decoder-Consistent Hamiltonians for POVM-Based Quantum Relaxations
summary: In compression-based quantum relaxations like QRAO, classical variables are encoded into qubits and decoded after optimization. We formalize that the choice of the quantum Hamiltonian is fundamentally determined by this decoder. By representing the decoder as a POVM, we define a unique decoder-consistent Hamiltonian via the pullback of the post-decoding expected objective value. Using this framework, we reveal that standard QRAO Hamiltonians are inconsistent for certain mixed-degree quadratic functions, and we provide new approximation guarantees for the MaxCut problem based directly on POVM decoder design.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes how decoders (as POVMs) determine quantum Hamiltonians in compression-based quantum relaxations (QRAO), reveals inconsistencies in standard Hamiltonians for mixed-degree quadratic functions, and provides new MaxCut approximation guarantees via POVM decoder design.
AI.motivation: To formalize the relationship between decoders and quantum Hamiltonians in quantum relaxation optimization (QRAO), and to identify and resolve inconsistencies in standard Hamiltonian constructions.
AI.method: The decoder is represented as a POVM, and the decoder-consistent Hamiltonian is defined via the pullback of the post-decoding expected objective value. This framework is applied to analyze standard QRAO Hamiltonians and to design new POVM-based decoders for MaxCut.
AI.result: Standard QRAO Hamiltonians are shown to be inconsistent for certain mixed-degree quadratic functions. New approximation guarantees for MaxCut are derived based directly on the POVM decoder design.
AI.conclusion: The POVM-based framework provides a principled way to construct consistent Hamiltonians for quantum relaxations and yields improved guarantees for combinatorial optimization problems like MaxCut.

title: Gauging the Spacetime Code
summary: In recent years, the spacetime code has arisen as a candidate for a unifying view of fault tolerance in space and time. On the other hand, the recent study of dynamical phases has increasingly turned its attention to fault tolerance as a notion of a dynamically stable process. In this work, I explore one pathway between the two, achieved by gauging the spacetime code. This gives rise to a lattice gauge theory that inherits the elements of fault tolerance associated with a circuit, with Gauss laws corresponding to equivalence relations between configurations of spacetime errors and Wilson loops corresponding to detectors. The obtained gauge theory finds a surprisingly wide array of applications, from quantum error correction to condensed matter physics, and even learning theory: (1) It contains in its description foliated computation, and hence gives rise to one version of a gauge theory for measurement-based quantum computation. (2) For a class of topologically ordered mixed states, it gives us a gauge-theoretic language to describe the classical memory associated with the state. (3) The gauge-invariant observables of the theory which describe detectors also coincide with the learnable degrees of freedom of circuit Pauli noise.

AI.tldr: This paper bridges spacetime codes and fault tolerance by gauging spacetime codes, producing a lattice gauge theory where Gauss laws correspond to error equivalence relations and Wilson loops act as detectors. This framework unifies applications in quantum error correction, condensed matter (topologically ordered mixed states), measurement-based quantum computation (foliated computation), and learning theory (identifying learnable Pauli noise degrees of freedom).
AI.motivation: To unify two perspectives on fault tolerance—spacetime codes (a unifying view of fault tolerance in space and time) and dynamical phases (fault tolerance as dynamical stability)—by developing a gauge-theoretic framework via gauging the spacetime code.
AI.method: Gauging the spacetime code to derive a lattice gauge theory; establishing Gauss laws as equivalence relations among spacetime error configurations and Wilson loops as detectors.
AI.result: The gauge theory yields: (1) a description of foliated computation (measurement-based quantum computation), (2) a gauge-theoretic language for classical memory in topologically ordered mixed states, and (3) gauge-invariant observables (detectors) coinciding with learnable degrees of freedom in circuit Pauli noise.
AI.conclusion: The gauged spacetime code framework provides a unified, cross-disciplinary language linking quantum error correction, condensed matter physics, and learning theory.

title: Learning Hamiltonians at Long Times
summary: We study the problem of learning an unknown $n$-qubit Hamiltonian $H$ from $U = e^{-iHt}$ for a single time $t$, where $t$ may be arbitrarily large. For broad families of local Hamiltonians, we prove that, with high probability over $H$ and $t$, any sum of local observables $A$ that is normalized and orthogonal to $H$ satisfies $\tfrac{1}{2^n}\|[U(t),A]\|_F^2 \geq 1/\text{poly}(n)$. The Hamiltonian is therefore the unique approximately conserved local observable, and we can efficiently recover $H$, up to scale, as the approximate null vector of a data matrix built from random product-state inputs and classical shadows. As a corollary, we obtain a weak equilibration statement: the infinite-temperature autocorrelation of every sum of local observables orthogonal to $H$ decays by at least an inverse-polynomial amount.

AI.tldr: For unknown n-qubit local Hamiltonians, any normalized local observable orthogonal to H must have a commutator squared Frobenius norm at least 1/poly(n), making H the unique approximately conserved local observable. This enables efficient Hamiltonian recovery via classical shadows and random product states, and implies weak equilibration (inverse-polynomial decay of infinite-temperature autocorrelations for observables orthogonal to H).
AI.motivation: To learn an unknown n-qubit Hamiltonian H from a single time-evolution unitary U = e^{-iHt} without requiring multiple times or prior knowledge of the Hamiltonian's structure, and to establish that H is essentially the only approximately conserved local observable.
AI.method: Proves that for broad families of local Hamiltonians, any sum of local observables A orthogonal to H satisfies a lower bound on the squared Frobenius norm of the commutator [U(t), A] (at least 1/poly(n)). Then uses random product-state inputs and classical shadows to build a data matrix whose approximate null vector recovers H up to scale.
AI.result: The Hamiltonian is the unique approximately conserved local observable (commutator lower bound). Efficient recovery of H from a single time t is possible. Weak equilibration follows: infinite-temperature autocorrelation of observables orthogonal to H decays by at least an inverse-polynomial amount.
AI.conclusion: Single-time Hamiltonian learning is feasible for local Hamiltonians, with rigorous guarantees, and this implies fundamental constraints on equilibration of local observables orthogonal to H.

title: Information-Geometric Bound on the Robustness of Entanglement Generation
summary: Entanglement generation is a central resource for quantum information processing, quantum networking, and quantum sensing. In practical implementations, however, entangling interactions are inevitably subject to uncertainty and fluctuations in the interaction strength. We investigate the robustness of entanglement generation in the presence of such imperfections and establish a direct connection between the robustness of entanglement generation and quantum Fisher information (QFI). For two interacting qubits, we show that the reduction in concurrence caused by fluctuations in the interaction parameter is bounded by the QFI with respect to the interaction strength.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how fluctuations in interaction strength affect entanglement generation in two-qubit systems, establishing that the degradation of concurrence due to such fluctuations is bounded by the quantum Fisher information with respect to the interaction parameter.
AI.motivation: Entanglement is a key resource for quantum technologies, but practical implementations suffer from uncertainty and fluctuations in interaction strength. The paper aims to understand and quantify the robustness of entanglement generation under such imperfections.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze two interacting qubits and derive a bound connecting the reduction in concurrence (an entanglement measure) caused by fluctuations in the interaction parameter to the quantum Fisher information (QFI) with respect to that interaction strength.
AI.result: For two interacting qubits, the reduction in concurrence caused by fluctuations in the interaction parameter is bounded by the QFI with respect to the interaction strength.
AI.conclusion: A direct connection is established between the robustness of entanglement generation and quantum Fisher information, providing a quantitative framework for understanding how interaction uncertainties affect entanglement generation.

title: Symmetries and overparametrization properties of Hamiltonian variational ansatzes for the $(1+1)$d $\mathbb{Z}_2$ lattice gauge theory
summary: We perform detailed studies of five Hamiltonian variational ansatzes (HVA) based on the Hamiltonian of the $(1+1)$d $\mathbb{Z}_2$ lattice gauge theory. The ansatzes are designed to respect local and global symmetries of the original Hamiltonian and therefore act on a finely segmented state Hilbert space. Following Larocca et al. (2023), we numerically study the dimension of the dynamical Lie algebra (DLA) and the rank of the quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) of the ansatzes within specific invariant subspaces. The ansatzes all involve sums of weight-three Paulis in their generators, which is a feature that have so far been underexplored in this context. We also perform numerical experiments to determine the ground state energy of the original Hamiltonian via variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), and observe that overparametrization of the ansatzes coincides with the apparent disappearance of local minima in the loss function, in line with the finding in the reference. Finally, the decay rate of the VQE loss function under gradient descent optimization is revealed to scale linearly with the number of parameters in the ansatz. These results help to enrich the theory of overparameterization of quantum circuits and inform the design of scalable variational ansatzes.

AI.tldr: This paper studies five Hamiltonian variational ansatzes (HVA) for (1+1)d Z₂ lattice gauge theory, analyzing their dynamical Lie algebra, quantum Fisher information matrix, overparameterization phenomena in VQE, and the linear scaling of loss decay rate with parameter count.
AI.motivation: To enrich the theory of overparameterization of quantum circuits and inform the design of scalable variational ansatzes, particularly for ansatzes involving weight-three Pauli generators that have been underexplored.
AI.method: The authors design five HVAs respecting local and global symmetries of the Z₂ lattice gauge theory Hamiltonian, numerically study the dimension of DLA and rank of QFIM within invariant subspaces, perform VQE experiments for ground state energy estimation, and analyze the loss function landscape under gradient descent.
AI.result: Overparameterization coincides with disappearance of local minima in the loss function; decay rate of VQE loss under gradient descent scales linearly with the number of parameters in the ansatz.
AI.conclusion: These findings enrich overparameterization theory for quantum circuits and provide guidance for designing scalable variational ansatzes with higher-weight Pauli generators.

title: Optimal convex approximation of quantum channels based on $α$-affinity
summary: Determining the minimal distance between a target channel and a convex hull of predefined set of implementable channels is a fundamental problem in quantum resource theory, and provides key guidance for experimental implementations. In this work, we develop a unified analytical framework for optimal convex approximation of quantum channels based on the quantum $α$-affinity measure. We construct a channel distance metric induced by the α-affinity and the ChoiJamiolkowski isomorphism, which satisfies the required properties of a well-defined channel distance. Subsequently, we present an optimization framework for the convex approximation of quantum channels, and derive analytical solutions for the optimal convex approximation of single-qubit unitary channels over both the SU(2)-covariant and Pauli channel families, obtaining closed-form expressions for the optimal parameters and the minimal approximation distance. This framework is further applied to the amplitude-damping channel, yielding the explicit form of its optimal approximation and the associated minimal α-affinity distance. In contrast to conventional approaches based on the diamond norm, our framework provides a systematic and analytically tractable approach to quantum channel approximation under realistic constraints.

AI.tldr: A unified analytical framework for optimal convex approximation of quantum channels is developed using quantum α-affinity measure, deriving closed-form solutions for single-qubit unitary channels over SU(2)-covariant and Pauli families, and applied to amplitude-damping channels, offering analytically tractable alternatives to diamond norm approaches.
AI.motivation: Determining minimal distance between a target channel and a convex hull of implementable channels is fundamental in quantum resource theory and provides key guidance for experimental implementations.
AI.method: Develops a unified analytical framework based on quantum α-affinity measure, constructs a channel distance metric via α-affinity and Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism, and derives analytical solutions for optimal convex approximation.
AI.result: Obtains closed-form expressions for optimal parameters and minimal approximation distance for single-qubit unitary channels over SU(2)-covariant and Pauli channel families; derives explicit optimal approximation form for amplitude-damping channels.
AI.conclusion: Provides a systematic and analytically tractable approach to quantum channel approximation under realistic constraints, contrasting favorably with conventional diamond norm approaches.

title: Tight relation between the physical effects of a quantum measurement and the information gained about an observable
summary: The dynamics of quantum measurements defines a precise relation between the information gained about one physical property of a system and the observable changes in another physical property of the same system. Here, we express this relation in terms of the Hilbert space superpositions of the corresponding eigenstates and show how the probability of an observable physical change can be obtained from the Bayesian update of the probabilities associated with the information obtained in the measurement. Our analysis demonstrates that the superposition principle provides the tightest possible expression of the trade-off between information and back action in a quantum measurement.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that the trade-off between information gain and back action in quantum measurements is fundamentally governed by the superposition principle, expressed through Hilbert space eigenstate superpositions and Bayesian probability updates.
AI.motivation: To establish a precise, quantitative relation between the information gained about one physical property and the observable changes in another property during quantum measurements, and to determine the fundamental limits of this trade-off.
AI.method: The authors express the measurement dynamics in terms of Hilbert space superpositions of eigenstates, and derive the probability of observable physical changes from Bayesian updates of measurement probabilities.
AI.result: The superposition principle provides the tightest possible expression of the trade-off between information and back action in quantum measurements.
AI.conclusion: The superposition principle sets the fundamental bound on the information-back action trade-off, with the Bayesian update framework providing a consistent probabilistic description of measurement-induced changes.

title: Periodic Symmetry-Adapted Encoding: Qubit Reduction in Crystalline Electronic Structure
summary: We extend the symmetry-adapted encoding (SAE) framework to periodic electronic structure, enabling qubit-efficient quantum simulation of crystalline materials. By constructing a $Γ$-point supercell Hamiltonian from a folded $k$-point calculation and systematically identifying all applicable space-group symmetry generators -- including spin-parity, point-group, and crystal translation symmetries -- we obtain qubit Hamiltonians with fewer qubits than the Jordan--Wigner starting point. We benchmark diamond, silicon, 3C-SiC, MgO, NaCl, CsCl, h-BN, wurtzite AlN, $α$-quartz SiO$_2$, and MgF$_2$ using active spaces chosen to preserve complete near-degenerate frontier manifolds across cubic, hexagonal, trigonal, and tetragonal space groups. Across the suite the periodic SAE removes 4--8 qubits. The B2 CsCl benchmark realises eight independent Boolean generators, i.e. a symmetry group isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}_2^8$, reducing CAS(6,7) from 14 to 6 qubits. This exceeds the $\mathbb{Z}_2^5$ maximum of molecular SAE, where only two spin parities and at most three independent Boolean point-group generators are available, because the folded crystal supplies three additional half-translation symmetries. Noiseless UCCSD-VQE benchmarks against exact diagonalisation in the active-space sector show that the reduced encodings preserve the target energies to well below chemical accuracy while reducing variational parameter counts by $3$--$8\times$ and CNOT counts by up to $309\times$. The largest circuit savings occur when translation and point-group generators act independently in the active space, demonstrating that periodic symmetry can be converted directly into both qubit and ansatz compression. The method is implemented in the open-source QuantumSymmetry package and requires no manual specification of symmetry generators.

AI.tldr: The paper extends symmetry-adapted encoding (SAE) to periodic systems, enabling qubit-efficient quantum simulation of crystalline materials by leveraging space-group symmetries including half-translations from folded crystals. Benchmarks on 10 materials show 4-8 qubit reductions, up to 309× CNOT savings, and 3-8× variational parameter reductions while preserving chemical accuracy.
AI.motivation: To enable qubit-efficient quantum simulation of periodic crystalline materials by extending the symmetry-adapted encoding framework beyond molecular systems, where the maximum symmetry group is limited to ℤ₂⁵, to crystalline systems where additional space-group symmetries (especially half-translations from folded crystals) can provide greater compression.
AI.method: Construct Γ-point supercell Hamiltonian from folded k-point calculation; systematically identify all applicable space-group symmetry generators (spin-parity, point-group, crystal translation symmetries); apply symmetry-adapted encoding to obtain reduced qubit Hamiltonians; benchmark using UCCSD-VQE with active spaces preserving complete near-degenerate frontier manifolds.
AI.result: Periodic SAE removes 4-8 qubits across 10 materials spanning cubic, hexagonal, trigonal, and tetragonal space groups. CsCl achieves 8 independent Boolean generators (ℤ₂⁸), reducing CAS(6,7) from 14 to 6 qubits. CNOT counts reduced by up to 309×, variational parameters by 3-8×, while preserving energies below chemical accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Periodic symmetry can be directly converted into both qubit and ansatz compression, with the largest circuit savings occurring when translation and point-group generators act independently in the active space. The method is implemented in the open-source QuantumSymmetry package with no manual specification of symmetry generators needed.

title: Engineered dissipation for faster adiabatic state preparation
summary: Adiabatic state preparation is often slowed by nonadiabatic leakage near small spectral gaps. We propose an engineered dissipative protocol that uses a filtered reservoir to induce predominantly downward transitions in the instantaneous energy eigenbasis while leaving the instantaneous ground state dark. The leaked population generated by nonadiabatic driving is therefore continuously relaxed back toward the low-energy sector. An effective avoided-crossing analysis shows that in the regime where the engineered relaxation strength is much larger than the minimum gap, the runtime scaling can improve from the closed-system behavior $\mathcal{O}(Δ^{-2})$ to $\mathcal{O}(Δ^{-1})$ Finite-temperature upward transitions introduce a thermal error floor, but the enhancement survives when this heating rate remains below the target error tolerance. Numerical results show improved ground-state preparation over closed-system annealing. We also discuss a possible superconducting-circuit implementation using structured bosonic reservoirs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an engineered dissipative protocol using a filtered reservoir to suppress nonadiabatic leakage in adiabatic state preparation, improving runtime scaling from O(Δ^{-2}) to O(Δ^{-1}) while maintaining ground-state fidelity.
AI.motivation: Adiabatic state preparation is often slowed by nonadiabatic leakage near small spectral gaps, motivating the need for a protocol that mitigates these errors without sacrificing runtime efficiency.
AI.method: The authors introduce an engineered dissipative protocol where a filtered reservoir induces predominantly downward transitions in the instantaneous energy eigenbasis, leaving the ground state dark. Nonadiabatic leakage is continuously relaxed back to the low-energy sector. An effective avoided-crossing analysis is performed, and a superconducting-circuit implementation using structured bosonic reservoirs is discussed.
AI.result: In the regime where engineered relaxation strength >> minimum gap, the runtime scaling improves from O(Δ^{-2}) (closed system) to O(Δ^{-1}). Finite-temperature upward transitions introduce a thermal error floor, but the enhancement persists when heating rate < error tolerance. Numerical results confirm improved ground-state preparation.
AI.conclusion: The dissipative protocol enhances adiabatic state preparation by leveraging engineered dissipation to overcome nonadiabatic errors, with potential experimental realization via superconducting circuits.

title: Symmetry-adapted qubit encoding with complete active space and Bravyi--Kitaev mapping for quantum chemistry on a quantum computer
summary: We present a symmetry-adapted qubit encoding with complete active space (SAE-CAS) for quantum chemistry on fault-tolerant and near-term quantum processors. Building on exact-symmetry encodings, we extend symmetry-adapted mappings to approximate $Z$-symmetries corresponding to frozen-core and virtual orbitals, thereby reducing qubit requirements without significant loss of accuracy. We derive the mapping from the second-quantised Hamiltonian to active-space qubit Hamiltonians, prove its equivalence to the canonical CAS Hamiltonian with frozen-core and virtual-orbital projection, and integrate it with point-group and spin-parity symmetry encodings via affine Clifford transformations to maximise qubit reduction while preserving the target symmetry sector. The same framework also accommodates the Bravyi--Kitaev mapping, yielding an SAE-CAS-BK variant that is unitarily equivalent to SAE-CAS. Numerical benchmarking on nine small molecules using UCCSD and a hardware-efficient shifted-circular-alternating (HE-SCA) ansatz shows that SAE-CAS reduces qubit counts and Pauli-operator weight, yields shallower circuits with fewer parameters, and often accelerates VQE convergence; with HE-SCA it consistently reaches CAS reference energies in cases where JW-CAS does not converge within the tested budgets. We provide an open-source implementation in the Python package QuantumSymmetry. SAE-CAS offers a route to resource-efficient molecular simulations on fault-tolerant and near-term quantum processors.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a symmetry-adapted qubit encoding with complete active space (SAE-CAS) that reduces qubit requirements for quantum chemistry simulations by encoding approximate Z-symmetries of frozen-core and virtual orbitals, while integrating point-group and spin-parity symmetries. Benchmarked on nine small molecules, it demonstrates reduced qubit counts, shallower circuits, and faster VQE convergence compared to standard encodings.
AI.motivation: To reduce qubit and circuit resource requirements for quantum chemistry simulations on near-term and fault-tolerant quantum processors, by extending symmetry-adapted encodings to approximate Z-symmetries of frozen-core and virtual orbitals without significant accuracy loss.
AI.method: SAE-CAS extends exact-symmetry qubit encodings to approximate Z-symmetries (frozen-core/virtual orbitals), derives the mapping from second-quantised to active-space qubit Hamiltonians, proves equivalence to canonical CAS with frozen-core/virtual-orbital projection, integrates point-group and spin-parity symmetries via affine Clifford transformations, and includes a Bravyi-Kitaev variant (SAE-CAS-BK). Benchmarked on nine small molecules using UCCSD and hardware-efficient shifted-circular-alternating (HE-SCA) ansatz.
AI.result: SAE-CAS reduces qubit counts and Pauli-operator weight, yields shallower circuits with fewer parameters, and accelerates VQE convergence. With HE-SCA, SAE-CAS consistently reaches CAS reference energies where JW-CAS fails to converge within tested budgets. Open-source implementation in Python package QuantumSymmetry.
AI.conclusion: SAE-CAS provides a resource-efficient approach to molecular simulations on fault-tolerant and near-term quantum processors, balancing qubit reduction and accuracy preservation.

title: No-go theorems on simulating uncertainty principle's signatures
summary: Uncertainty principle, one of the most iconic features of quantum mechanics, was originally viewed as a fundamental limitation. Since the inception of quantum information science, researchers began to use it to achieve quantum advantages. To better understand the origin of these advantages, an essential question is: To what extent can the uncertainty principle's signatures be simulated by a single measurement? As a single measurement clearly cannot demonstrate the uncertainty principle, such a simulation, if exists, implies the claimed advantages may either stem from other quantum features, or just be reproducible in a less resourceful way. In this work, we report a series of noise-robust no-go theorems, showing that strong enough signatures of uncertainty principle cannot be simulated by a single measurement, even when assisted by quantum pre- or post-processing. This signature is modelled by complementary instruments. We completely characterise complementary instruments by a numerically feasible measure and show that they are necessary and sufficient resources for the advantage in an operational task that aims to unambiguously send classical information.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that strong signatures of the uncertainty principle cannot be simulated by a single measurement, even with quantum pre- or post-processing, and characterizes complementary instruments as necessary and sufficient resources for advantages in sending classical information unambiguously.
AI.motivation: To understand whether quantum advantages attributed to the uncertainty principle can be simulated by a single measurement, thereby clarifying the origin of quantum advantages in quantum information science.
AI.method: The authors develop noise-robust no-go theorems and completely characterize complementary instruments using a numerically feasible measure.
AI.result: Strong signatures of the uncertainty principle cannot be simulated by a single measurement, even with quantum pre- or post-processing assistance. Complementary instruments are fully characterized and shown to be necessary and sufficient resources for unambiguous classical information transmission tasks.
AI.conclusion: The uncertainty principle provides genuine non-classical resources that cannot be reduced to single-measurement simulations, and complementary instruments capture the essential operational resource for certain quantum communication advantages.

title: Non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics of a memory-bearing open-system process
summary: We show the emergence of memory effects in the dynamics of a driven two-level system interacting with a composite environment, and analyze their influence on work, heat and entropy production. We further investigate how the interplay between driving, dissipation and memory effects, stemming from the finiteness of the environment, shapes the thermodynamic response of the system, thus providing insight into quantum thermodynamics beyond the Markovian approximation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates memory effects (non-Markovian dynamics) in a driven two-level system coupled to a composite environment, analyzing their impact on work, heat, and entropy production, and exploring how driving, dissipation, and finite-environment memory shape quantum thermodynamic behavior beyond standard Markovian approximations.
AI.motivation: To understand how memory effects arising from a finite, composite environment influence thermodynamic quantities (work, heat, entropy) in driven quantum systems, extending quantum thermodynamics beyond the Markovian limit.
AI.method: The authors study a driven two-level system interacting with a composite environment, analyzing the dynamics to reveal memory effects and their thermodynamic consequences using a non-Markovian framework.
AI.result: Memory effects emerge from the finiteness of the environment, and the interplay between driving, dissipation, and these non-Markovian effects significantly shapes the thermodynamic response (work, heat, entropy production) of the system.
AI.conclusion: The work provides insight into quantum thermodynamics beyond the Markovian approximation, highlighting the critical role of environmental memory in determining thermodynamic behavior.

title: Broadband AC Magnetic Field Sensing via Continuous wave optically detected magnetic resonance with NV Centers in diamond
summary: The nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond has attracted considerable attention as a highly sensitive quantum sensor that can operate at room temperature. In particular, continuous-wave optically detected magnetic resonance (CW-ODMR) is promising for a wide range of applications because of its simplicity. However, conventional AC magnetic-field sensing schemes based on CW-ODMR suffer from a limited detection bandwidth: the detectable frequency is either fixed by intrinsic physical parameters of the NV center or, even when tunable, restricted to a narrow range of only a few MHz. Here, we propose a broadband AC magnetometry scheme based on CW-ODMR with NV centers using microwave-driven dressed states.Through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, we show that the proposed scheme enables the detection of AC magnetic fields with frequencies up to the order of 100 MHz, which has been difficult to achieve using conventional CW-ODMR-based methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a broadband AC magnetometry scheme using NV centers in diamond with CW-ODMR and microwave-driven dressed states, enabling detection of AC magnetic fields up to ~100 MHz, overcoming the limited bandwidth of conventional methods.
AI.motivation: Conventional CW-ODMR-based AC magnetic-field sensing schemes suffer from limited detection bandwidth, where the detectable frequency is either fixed or restricted to a narrow range of only a few MHz.
AI.method: The authors propose a broadband AC magnetometry scheme based on CW-ODMR with NV centers using microwave-driven dressed states, supported by theoretical analysis and numerical simulations.
AI.result: The proposed scheme enables detection of AC magnetic fields with frequencies up to the order of 100 MHz, which has been difficult to achieve using conventional CW-ODMR-based methods.
AI.conclusion: The broadband AC magnetometry scheme using dressed states significantly extends the detection bandwidth of CW-ODMR-based NV center sensors, making them more versatile for practical applications.

title: Double-bracket quantum algorithms for thermal state preparation
summary: We propose quantum algorithms for preparing thermal states via the simulation of the thermofield double states. The key idea is to leverage double-bracket quantum algorithms to implement imaginary-time evolution on thermofield double states, whose reduced state realizes the Gibbs state. Our method, termed double-bracket thermofield double (DB-TFD), introduces two variants. The first, the vanilla DB-TFD algorithm, directly implements imaginary-time evolution using double-bracket quantum imaginary-time evolution. The second, poly DB-TFD, employs double-bracket quantum signal processing to approximate the imaginary-time evolution operator via a polynomial transformation. We demonstrate that the complexity of the poly DB-TFD algorithm scales exponentially with the inverse temperature in a broad practical regime. This scaling is consistent with existing methods, and numerical simulations support the corresponding theoretical bound. We further demonstrate the utility of DB-TFD in quantum Boltzmann machines for generative modeling, achieving improved performance compared with variational imaginary-time evolution approaches. These results establish DB-TFD as a promising route for thermal state preparation in the near-term and early-fault-tolerant regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes double-bracket thermofield double (DB-TFD) algorithms for preparing thermal (Gibbs) states by simulating imaginary-time evolution on thermofield double states. Two variants are introduced: vanilla DB-TFD (direct imaginary-time evolution) and poly DB-TFD (polynomial approximation via quantum signal processing). Poly DB-TFD scales exponentially with inverse temperature, matching existing methods, and shows improved performance over variational approaches in quantum Boltzmann machines.
AI.motivation: To develop efficient quantum algorithms for preparing thermal states (Gibbs states), which are essential for quantum statistical mechanics, open quantum systems, and quantum machine learning applications like Boltzmann machines.
AI.method: Two DB-TFD variants: (1) vanilla DB-TFD using double-bracket quantum imaginary-time evolution directly; (2) poly DB-TFD using double-bracket quantum signal processing to approximate imaginary-time evolution via polynomial transformations.
AI.result: Poly DB-TFD complexity scales exponentially with inverse temperature in a broad practical regime, consistent with existing methods, with numerical simulations supporting the theoretical bound. DB-TFD achieves improved performance over variational imaginary-time evolution in quantum Boltzmann machines.
AI.conclusion: DB-TFD is a promising route for thermal state preparation suitable for near-term and early-fault-tolerant quantum regimes.

title: Magnetic flux as a quantized Lorentz pseudoscalar and its relation to electric charge quantization
summary: In this paper, we re-examine the well-known question of why electric charges exist only in quantized portions. In this context, we revisit the motion of a charged particle in a field-free region around a current-carrying solenoid. Solving the corresponding Schrödinger equation leads to a simultaneous quantization condition for the magnetic flux and the electric charge. We also demonstrate the Lorentz invariance of this condition by showing that the magnetic flux behaves like a pseudoscalar under Lorentz transformations.

AI.tldr: This paper re-examines charge quantization by analyzing a charged particle moving in a field-free region around a solenoid, deriving a simultaneous quantization condition for magnetic flux and electric charge from the Schrödinger equation, and demonstrating its Lorentz invariance.
AI.motivation: To re-examine the fundamental question of why electric charge exists only in quantized portions.
AI.method: Solving the Schrödinger equation for a charged particle in a field-free region around a current-carrying solenoid, and analyzing the Lorentz transformation properties of magnetic flux.
AI.result: A simultaneous quantization condition linking magnetic flux and electric charge; demonstration that magnetic flux behaves like a pseudoscalar under Lorentz transformations, confirming Lorentz invariance of the condition.
AI.conclusion: The quantization of electric charge is intrinsically connected to magnetic flux quantization, and the derived condition is Lorentz invariant.

title: Shattering the Symmetry Trap in Fixed-Ansatz VQE: An Accelerated ADAPT-VQE Study of Three Pillar Molecules under Bravyi-Kitaev Mapping
comment: 8 pages, including raw algorithmic telemetry logs
summary: Fixed-ansatz Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQE), such as the Unitary Coupled Cluster with Singles and Doubles (UCCSD) framework, frequently suffer from severe initialization paralyzation and zero-gradient traps when evaluated using the non-local Bravyi-Kitaev (BK) fermion-to-qubit mapping. In this work, we systematically demonstrate how the Adaptive Derivative-Assembled Pseudo-Trotter (ADAPT-VQE) framework shatters these structural limitations across three distinct electronic and geometric molecular pillars: Lithium Hydride ($\text{LiH}$), Hydrogen Fluoride ($\text{HF}$), and Water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$), under heavily stretched or asymmetric multi-reference configurations. While conventional UCCSD-VQE flatlines completely at a zero energy shift ($0.000000$~Ha) due to global phase cancellations inherent to the BK tree structures, our dynamic ADAPT-VQE loop successfully isolates the dominant symmetry-breaking operators using analytical commutator gradients. To bypass the severe $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ computational bottlenecks of dense matrix exponentiation and Singular Value Decomposition on larger registers, we implement a highly optimized, vector-based Taylor series expansion state-evolution engine. Our numerical results show that the accelerated ADAPT-VQE framework achieves instant, exact Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) convergence within the very first macro-cycle across all three molecular systems, maintaining absolute numerical stability up to a 12-qubit register space. This study establishes a robust, hardware-efficient path for simulating strongly correlated, highly polarized triatomic chemical environments on near-term local architectures.

AI.tldr: ADAPT-VQE overcomes initialization paralysis and zero-gradient traps that plague fixed-ansatz UCCSD-VQE under Bravyi-Kitaev mapping, achieving instant FCI convergence across LiH, HF, and H₂O in stretched multi-reference configurations using analytical commutator gradients and an optimized Taylor-series state-evolution engine.
AI.motivation: Fixed-ansatz VQE (e.g., UCCSD) suffers from severe initialization paralysis and zero-gradient traps when using Bravyi-Kitaev fermion-to-qubit mapping, preventing convergence in strongly correlated molecular systems.
AI.method: ADAPT-VQE with analytical commutator gradients to dynamically isolate dominant symmetry-breaking operators; vector-based Taylor series expansion state-evolution engine replaces dense matrix exponentiation and SVD to bypass O(N³) bottlenecks.
AI.result: Accelerated ADAPT-VQE achieves instant, exact FCI convergence within the first macro-cycle across LiH, HF, and H₂O, maintaining absolute numerical stability up to 12 qubits.
AI.conclusion: ADAPT-VQE provides a robust, hardware-efficient pathway for simulating strongly correlated, highly polarized triatomic systems on near-term quantum architectures.

title: Rapid Gaussian Boson Sampling Circuit Screening for GKP States Creation via a Two-Stage Machine Learning Surrogate
summary: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are essential non-Gaussian resources for fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, enabling logical qubit encoding with intrinsic robustness against errors. Several approaches to GKP state preparation have been explored, including measurement-based protocols in circuit QED and trapped-ion systems, cat-state breeding, and photon-subtraction schemes. However, these methods are either restricted to specific platforms or require deep non-Gaussian resource chains with exponentially low success probabilities. Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) offers a compelling all-photonic alternative by generating non-Gaussian states through measurement-induced nonlinearity, without the need for matter-based ancilla or active feedforward. Nevertheless, its practical implementation is limited by the exponential computational cost of evaluating matrix hafnians-#P-complete functions that govern photon-number probabilities. To address this challenge, we introduce a two-stage Histogram Gradient Boosting surrogate pipeline that predicts, without any hafnian computation, the optimal heralding pattern, circuit fidelity, and post-selection probability for candidate GBS circuits, while reserving exact quantum simulation exclusively for surrogate-selected candidates. Trained on circuit configurations across 3-5 optical modes, the surrogate achieves 90.0% GKP-detection accuracy on a held-out set, representing a 23.7 percentage-point improvement over the baseline, with a fidelity mean absolute error of 0.032 and a log-scale post-selection probability $R^2 = 0.837$, reducing the total simulation burden by approximately 90%.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a machine learning surrogate (Histogram Gradient Boosting) to replace expensive hafnian computations in Gaussian Boson Sampling, accelerating the identification of optimal circuits for GKP state preparation by ~90% while maintaining high accuracy (90% GKP-detection, 0.032 fidelity MAE).
AI.motivation: Existing GKP state preparation methods (measurement-based, cat-breeding, photon-subtraction) are platform-specific or suffer from exponentially low success probabilities. GBS offers a compelling all-photonic alternative but is bottlenecked by the #P-complete hafnian computation required for optimizing circuit parameters.
AI.method: A two-stage Histogram Gradient Boosting surrogate pipeline: first predicts optimal heralding patterns, circuit fidelity, and post-selection probability for GBS circuits without hafnian computation; then reserves exact quantum simulation exclusively for surrogate-selected candidates. Trained on 3-5 optical mode configurations.
